transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-10
Start: 2027-02-10T15:30:00-08:00
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Oliver Hayes (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Luca Marino (CTO, Evoke AI), Priya Patel (Infra Lead, Evoke), Sam O'Neill (SRE, Evoke)

Auto-generated summary: (may be rough)
Evoke needs a reserved capacity option with strict SLOs (50-100ms p95 for short chat completions, 300-500ms p99 for longer contexts), plus encryption-at-rest and envelope encryption for model artifacts. They want a hybrid approach: mostly Dedicated with hosted fallback for spikes. Main asks: hot pool sizing, prewarm timing, burst guardrails, KMS integration, audit logs.

Topics covered:
- Latency SLOs and percentiles
- Prewarm / hot-warm pool strategies
- Fallback to hosted variants and cost tradeoffs
- Encryption and KMS/HSM model key handling
- Pilot and benchmark plan

Transcript body:
[00:00] Oliver (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intros, we'll let Evan from Evoke intro their use case and then Maya will take the deep end on prewarm/burst mechanics.
[00:18] Luca (Evoke CTO): Hi, yeah thanks. I'm Luca, CTO at Evoke. We're building a multimodal customer support assistant, lots of short-turn chat, occasional longer context retrievals. Our SLOs are pretty strict bc we compete on latency.
[00:31] Priya (Infra): Priya here — we own infra; our security team will require envelope encryption for models and keys kept in our KMS, and audit logs for token-level usage. we also need VPC peering with restricted egress.
[00:45] Maya (Redwood SE): Great — those are all totally in scope. quick question, Luca: what's your p95 target for typical chat responses today?
[00:52] Luca: Right now p95 is about 120ms on our existing smaller models but that's with lots of caching and aggressive batching. For production we want to be under 100ms p95 for the 90% of queries and p99 under 400ms for longer prompts.
[01:10] Sam (SRE): And to add, our traffic profile is spiky — marketing launches cause 10x bursts that last 20-30 minutes. we want to avoid cold-starts causing SLA misses.
[01:22] Oliver: That's helpful. so we usually recommend a hybrid reserved plus hosted fallback. dedicated GPUs for steady-state with a small 'hot pool' to cover base throughput, and then prewarm windows and hosted fallback for large spikes. Maya, do you want to walk through sizing heuristics?
[01:35] Maya: Sure — what we usually do is look at sustained RPS and p95 latency target to size the hot pool. then we decide how much warm capacity to keep idle vs prewarm on schedule. For Evoke's 10x burst profile, I'd recommend a hot pool that covers 2-3x normal, and an autoscale buffer that pulls from a warm pool prewarmed to 50% so you can ramp quickly.
[01:58] Luca: 2-3x hot pool — that sounds like a lot of reserved GPUs. our finance lead will push back. are there tradeoffs with smaller hot pool + faster fallback?
[02:10] Maya: yes; smaller hot pool means more reliance on hosted fallback which can add cross-region egress and slightly higher latency. also cost per token can rise. you can mitigate with KV prefix caching for common prompts which cuts repeat token cost, but it doesn't help cold-starts for new sessions.
[02:30] Priya: On the encryption side, we cannot expose model keys to Redwood-managed control plane. we can integrate with Redwood's private mode VPC and use our KMS via customer-managed key wrap. is that supported?
[02:43] Oliver: Yes — Redwood Private supports customer KMS/HSM integrations and key wrap for model artifacts; there are a few implementation patterns. Maya, do you want to note the UX differences?
[02:52] Maya: Sure — with Private you run the inference nodes in your VPC and we can integrate with your KMS so model keys never leave. Audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM. the tradeoff is slower rollout cadence and more ops on your side. for Dedicated we also support bringing-your-own-KMS with a key-encryption-key flow. sometimes customers pick Dedicated with private KMS for the best of both worlds.
[03:15] Sam: Would bringing our KMS impact failover to hosted fallback? if keys are in our KMS and hosted needs to take traffic, how does that work?
[03:25] Maya: Good question — we do not have hosted access to customer KMS in Private mode. the fallback approach is to use a model variant that doesn't require the same customer-managed key — e.g., a cached quantized copy or a Redwood-verified equivalent. this is a graceful degradation strategy: different model variant, similar quality but with managed keys.
[03:48] Luca: So in practice, during a large marketing spike we'd accept slightly different model behavior if it keeps latency under SLO?
[03:55] Oliver: Exactly — we pair fallbacks with canary policies and quality regressions guards so you get alerts if fallback responses deviate significantly.
[04:07] [Speaker 1]: (laughter) okay.
[04:10] Priya: Another thought: our compliance team will want per-tenant auditability and retention controls for the logs. can we set retention to 90 days and have logs routed to our S3?
[04:20] Maya: Yes — retention is configurable in the control plane and logs can be streamed to your S3 or to a SIEM via webhook. there are retention tiers for Dedicated/Private.
[04:28] Luca: Let's talk numbers — what would a pilot look like? we want to validate cold-start behavior and prewarm timing with our real traffic.
[04:36] Maya: Pilot approach: 1) Redwood provisions a Dedicated reserved pool sized for steady-state with a 2-node hot pool; 2) run a 2-hour benchmark using representative traffic trace that Luca shares; 3) measure p95/p99 and observe fallback behavior under induced spike; 4) tune prewarm windows and KV cache settings. We can do this in a staging VPC with KMS stubs.
[04:58] Oliver: Costwise we'll provide two buckets: committed reserved cost for Dedicated and delta for hosted fallback per token. We'll also surface what prewarm costs look like since keeping a large hot pool idle has a cost.
[05:12] Priya: On the security sheet, please include SOC2 scope, ISO certs, and how audit logs are signed. We need that for our procurement.
[05:20] Oliver: We'll attach our security pack after the call.
[05:25] [00:05:30] Luca: quick question about KV cache — do you support prefix-only caching? our prompts have stable prefixes for many flows.
[05:36] Maya: Yes — we support prefix and session-level KV cache strategies. prefix caching is very effective for chat applications with templated prompts. it cuts token compute almost entirely for repeated prefixes. be mindful of consistency if you push model updates; you may want to invalidate prefixes during rollouts.
[05:56] Sam: For rollouts we need an A/B approach with fallback to golden model on mismatch. do you support that?
[06:05] Maya: We do — our rollouts let you route a percent of traffic to a canary, and we can automatically rollback on quality regression or latency spikes. you can also pin specific users or tokens to a model version.
[06:18] [00:06:30] Luca: what about warm pool prewarm timings? if a burst can be predicted (marketing blast), can we schedule prewarm windows to start 10 minutes prior?
[06:28] Maya: Yes — you can schedule prewarm operations or trigger them via API. prewarming is fastest when you seed KV cache and keep GPUs at a low warm level rather than fully idle. seeding with common prompts reduces ramp time significantly.
[06:42] Priya: Any limitations on model size for prewarm? we use a 30B parameter model for ranked responses and a smaller 7B for chat. prewarming multiple models increases footprint.
[06:53] Maya: Larger models obviously consume more memory and GPU. recommended: keep the 30B loaded in a dedicated node if it's critical, and use quantized 7B for burst fallback. we can recommend a fleet mix: a couple of high-memory nodes and several smaller quantized nodes to trade off latency and cost.
[07:10] Oliver: Could we sketch a candidate configuration live? say steady-state RPS ~50, burst up to 500 for 25 minutes.
[07:20] Maya: For 50 RPS steady with p95 <100ms you'd probably need 2 high-memory GPUs in hot pool (for 30B) and 4 smaller GPUs handling 7B quantized for chat concurrency, plus a warm pool of 6 instances that can be prewarmed to 50% within 5 minutes. Fallback to hosted would cover anything beyond that.
[07:44] Luca: That's clearer. Finance will push on the 2 high-memory GPUs. can you show delta if we keep one high-memory and rely more on prewarm?
[07:55] Maya: If you keep one high-memory node, expect p95 to inch up and p99 to increase during sustained bursts, but you can tune prewarm aggressiveness. it's a classic latency vs cost tradeoff.
[08:06] [00:08:30] Priya: On the compliance note — do you have options for customer-managed logging keys or log signing?
[08:16] Maya: Yes — logs can be signed with your KMS and forwarded. we also support immutable append-only audit streams for compliance.
[08:24] Sam: A practical question: during a real-world spike do you wire traffic at the load balancer level or do you rely on smart routing from Redwood control plane? how does routing latency factor in?
[08:36] Oliver: Typically traffic is routed via the control plane which does policy routing; in Private deployments you can route directly with a local control plane to reduce hop latency. routing adds a small fixed overhead, usually single-digit milliseconds.
[08:49] Maya: For ultra-low latency you might colocate a lightweight edge router in your VPC to avoid cross-VPC hops. we can help recommend an architecture.
[08:59] Luca: Ok, let's discuss SLA penalties — what uptime/latency commitments are realistic for Dedicated?
[09:08] Maya: Dedicated customers get SLA-backed uptime and latency SLOs are defined in the contract. penalties are typically credits based on missed p95 targets across a billing period. we'll share standard language but it's negotiable for larger commitments.
[09:22] [00:09:30] Priya: For procurement we'll need an exportable statement of work that includes responsibilities matrix — who manages what during a failover?
[09:32] Oliver: We'll include an RACI and failover playbook in the pilot proposal.
[09:37] Maya: One more note — network egress costs during fallback to hosted can be material if you have large context windows and attachments. consider keeping attachments in your S3 and sending pointers to reduce token transfer.
[09:53] Sam: Good point. we do send images occasionally. what's the best pattern?
[09:59] Maya: Keep blobs in your S3 and send signed URLs; Redwood can retrieve or you can proxy them. that avoids tokenizing large binary content.
[10:10] [00:10:30] Luca: Let's surface the acceptance criteria for the pilot: p95 < 100ms for chat flows, p99 < 400ms for long flows, smooth fallback with less than 2x latency penalty, and no exposure of model keys outside our KMS.
[10:24] Oliver: Good checklist. Maya, we'll use those as pilot success metrics.
[10:29] Maya: I'll add thresholds to the pilot plan.
[10:33] [00:10:45] Priya: procurement also wants to see our data residency controls; we need logs and telemetry to remain in our chosen region.
[10:42] Oliver: Region pinning is supported for Dedicated and Private. Hosted has region options but not as strict as Private where you control network.
[10:51] Sam: if we do a hybrid route, how are rate limits enforced to prevent noisy tenants from stealing capacity?
[10:59] Maya: We enforce token-level rate limits and tenant-level throttles. in Dedicated you get isolation at the GPU pool level; in a shared warm pool we apply soft quotas and throttles to prioritize reserved customers.
[11:15] [00:11:30] Luca: Are there any pitfalls you've seen with marketing spikes specifically?
[11:21] Maya: Two common pitfalls — underestimating KV cache cold miss rates, and not seeding prewarm with correct prompt mix. both lead to worse-than-expected ramp times. so sharing representative traces is crucial.
[11:36] Priya: we'll provide 14 days of traces and an anonymized prompt set.
[11:40] Oliver: Great. we'll also request a sample model container so Maya can run a preliminary estimate locally.
[11:47] [00:12:00] Maya: I'll outline a pilot workbook — sections: traffic ingest, model mix, warm/hot sizing, KMS/keys design, rollback / fallbacks, metrics to capture.
[12:00] Luca: Timeline? we'd like to run pilot in 3 weeks to align with a planned product demo campaign.
[12:07] Oliver: We can aim for pilot start in three weeks if traces and sample model arrive by Feb 14th.
[12:13] Maya: For the benchmark we need a 2-hour window at peak synthetic load and a 30-minute long-run to capture p99 under churn.
[12:22] [00:12:30] Priya: Who will own the test harness? Evoke or Redwood?
[12:26] Maya: We can provide a harness and scripts; Evoke will run them in staging with Redwood observing. alternatively Redwood can run them in a staging VPC if you prefer.
[12:37] Sam: Let's do Evoke-run with Redwood monitoring — faster for us.
[12:40] [00:12:50] Luca: a couple of quick policy questions: do you support SAML SSO for the console and granular RBAC?
[12:48] Oliver: Yes — SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC are part of the enterprise bundle.
[12:54] Priya: also need request-level redaction for PII — is that doable?
[12:59] Maya: We support redaction hooks and pre-ingest rules. you can also route sensitive traffic to Private where data never leaves your VPC.
[13:09] [00:13:30] Luca: ok last architecture question — for the hosted fallback, is the model exactly the same as Dedicated or do you recommend a compressed variant?
[13:18] Maya: Usually compressed or quantized variant to reduce hosting cost and start-up time. we keep a compatibility matrix to ensure output parity within acceptable tolerances.
[13:29] Oliver: Any more questions before we wrap?
[13:33] Priya: procurement will want to see redwood's SOC2 and network diagrams.
[13:38] Oliver: We'll attach that pack and a proposed SOW.
[13:43] Luca: fine. Thanks all.
[13:46] [00:14:00] (wrap-up)
[14:02] Oliver: Recap of next steps: Evoke sends traces + sample model by Feb 14; Redwood sends pilot plan and pricing by Feb 17; Maya will schedule the benchmark and send scripts. action items in the notes.
[14:20] Priya: I'll be the point on security, Luca will own acceptance and Sam will run tests.
[14:25] Oliver: Great — I'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark window. thanks everyone.
[14:30] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker mislabels. some technical terms transcribed as 'K-V cash' or 'dedicate' in auto transcript.
